images.description: The Pung cholom is a Manipuri dance. It is the soul of Manipuri Sankirtana music and Classical Manipuri dance. The Pung Cholom is a unique classical dance of Manipur. This dance may be performed by men or women and is usually a prelude to the Ras Lila. In this style, the dancers play the pung (a form of hand beaten drum) while they dance at the same time. Dancers need to be graceful and acrobatic

images.title: File:Lai Haraoba-3 - 5571676820.jpg
images.description: Lai Haraoba is a public festival in Manipur, India celebrated to please traditional deities. The festival is in part a recollection of the creation stories played the deities with the first origin of this universe and evolution of the plants and animals through the will of Atiya Shidaba.[1] Translated, Lai Haraoba means "merry making of the Gods."[

profile.name: Thougal Jagoi
profile.tagline: A sacred Meitei dance of dedication performed to invoke deities during Lai Haraoba.
profile.insight: Dancers are strictly forbidden from making eye contact with the audience, as failing to maintain this boundary is considered a sacrilege against the deities being invoked.
profile.profile: Thougal Jagoi, also known as Jagoi Ashangbi, is a traditional Meitei dance performed by men, women, and maibis (priestesses) during the Lai Haraoba festival. This invocation lasts for thirty minutes and serves as a formal prelude to the Hoi Lauba ceremony. The dance is characterized by strict ritual protocols, including a prohibition on eye contact with observers.
profile.profile_long: Thougal Jagoi, also referred to as Jagoi Ashangbi, is a traditional dance form originating from the Meitei culture of Manipur. It is deeply embedded in the religious framework of the Lai Haraoba festival, a communal event dedicated to the worship of deities. The dance is performed by a collective of men, women, and maibis, who are the traditional priestesses of the Meitei people. The performance is structured as an act of dedication and invocation, intended to call upon the deities. The duration of the dance is fixed at thirty minutes, acting as a functional prelude to the subsequent Hoi Lauba ceremony. The performance is governed by strict ritual guidelines, most notably the prohibition of eye contact between the dancers and the audience. This rule is not merely a stylistic choice but a fundamental requirement of the ritual; any deviation from this standard is regarded as a sacrilege. As a form of folk dance within the Meitei tradition, it remains a living practice tied to the religious life of the community. While the dance is a recognized part of the Meitei cultural wealth, specific technical details regarding the choreography, musical accompaniment, and costume requirements for this particular variant are not documented in the sources.
